reason: Sunlight heats ocean water and should start the evaporation stage of the water cycle.
expectation: The Sun will cause ocean water to evaporate, possibly forming clouds.

effect: Evaporation provides water vapour for the next stage of the water cycle, while leaving salts in the ocean.
reaction: The distinction between invisible vapour and a visible cloud is useful.
reason: Cooling water vapour with air is a plausible way to form clouds and eventually rain.
expectation: The vapour will cool and condense into a cloud.

effect: Cooling moist air produced clouds, setting up the rain stage of the cycle.
reaction: The distinction between vapour and cloud droplets is reinforced.
reason: Clouds need to produce rain over land to create rivers and return water to the sea.
expectation: The clouds will bring rain to the land.

alternatives.reason: I could check its available partners if the land combination is wrong.

effect: Clouds combined with Water automatically to produce rainfall over land, so the next step is to collect or channel it.
reaction: I expected land to trigger rain, but the compatibility feedback made the intended pairing clear.
reason: Rain falling on the stone crust may collect and flow toward the sea.
expectation: The rainfall will form flowing water or channels on the rocky land.

effect: Rainfall on the crust formed rivers, which can carry sediment toward the ocean.
reaction: The explanation connects river flow with both erosion and deposition.
reason: A river meeting the ocean is a natural place for sediment to accumulate into a delta, and it returns water to the sea.
expectation: The rivers will deliver water and sediment to the ocean, potentially forming a delta and completing the cycle.

effect: Rivers cannot combine directly with the ocean; their available partners are Earth and Sun.
reaction: I expected the river–ocean meeting to form the delta, so the available pairings are surprising.
reason: Earth is the more plausible partner for adding sediment to the rivers and building a delta.
expectation: The rivers will carry sediment from the land and deposit it as a delta.

alternatives.reason: Sun may help complete the water cycle, but Earth seems more relevant to sediment.

effect: Earth and rivers produced sediment, which can now be deposited to build a delta.
reaction: The result clarifies the intermediate step I had skipped.
reason: Sediment deposited where rivers meet the ocean can build a delta.
expectation: The sediment will accumulate at the coast to form a delta.

alternatives.reason: This may complete the water cycle, but the sediment suggests finishing the delta first.

effect: Sediment combined automatically with Rivers to form a delta, completing that goal.
reaction: The slowing flow and branching deposits make the delta formation clear.
reason: Rivers previously listed Sun as an available partner, and the remaining goal is to complete the water cycle.
expectation: Sunlight will help return river water to the atmosphere and complete the cycle.

effect: The final combination completed the water cycle and clarified the roles of sunlight and gravity in moving water through it.
reaction: It was satisfying to see the stages brought together in one explanation.

mostWorthwhile.text: Making the delta was most worthwhile: the explanation connected slowing river flow, sediment deposition and branching channels to the formation of new land.

leastWorthwhile.text: The unsuccessful river–ocean attempt was the least useful moment on its own, though its compatibility feedback pointed toward the remaining recipes.

surprise.text: I expected clouds to combine with land to make rain, but Water was the required partner; the feedback automatically made rainfall.

arbitrary.text: Using Sun with Rivers to finish the cycle felt somewhat abstract: I followed the compatibility hint, although the final explanation made sunlight's role in evaporation clear.

continue.text: Yes. I would be interested in another chapter because the delta and water-cycle explanations connected the combinations to understandable physical processes.
